title: Cluster headache: recognising attacks and arranging effective treatment
intro: Cluster headache is a disorder causing exceptionally severe attacks, usually around an eye or temple on one side. Attacks tend to occur repeatedly during active periods, sometimes at similar times of day, with quieter periods between; some people have a more continuous pattern. Effective attack and preventive treatments exist. A first or changed severe headache needs assessment because other illnesses can resemble cluster headache.

sections.heading: What an attack can look like
paragraphs: The pain rises rapidly and may be burning, piercing or sharp. The eye on the painful side may water or become red, the eyelid may swell or droop and the nose may run or block. People often feel restless and move around rather than lying quietly. Attacks can recur during the day or wake someone from sleep. This pattern helps the clinician, but does not make self-diagnosis safe. Record the start, duration, side, associated symptoms and any treatment response.

sections.heading: Diagnosis includes checking for warning signs
paragraphs: A clinician takes a detailed history and examines the nervous system and eyes; specialist assessment and imaging may be needed to exclude another cause. Seek emergency help for a sudden explosive headache, new weakness, confusion, loss of vision or a new drooping eyelid or unequal pupils, even with a past cluster diagnosis. Fever with a stiff neck also needs urgent assessment. A painful red eye with altered vision should not simply be assumed to be a familiar attack. Report a different pattern or treatment that has stopped working.

sections.heading: Attack treatment must act quickly
paragraphs: Prescribed oxygen through the appropriate mask and an injected or nasal triptan are established attack treatments. Ordinary painkillers and tablets that act too slowly are not substitutes for a specific cluster plan. Suitability of a triptan depends on health conditions and other medicines. Oxygen equipment needs a prescription, training and fire-safety precautions; never smoke or allow flames near it. Do not improvise with someone else's equipment or increase doses yourself. Ask how to access treatment at home, at work and during travel.

sections.heading: Prevention is different from stopping an individual attack
paragraphs: A specialist may use preventive medicine, often verapamil, to reduce attacks during an active period. It requires careful prescribing and heart-tracing monitoring because it can affect cardiac conduction. A short bridging treatment or other options may be considered while prevention takes effect or if it is unsuitable. The choice, monitoring and stopping plan are individual. Some people identify alcohol as an attack trigger during a cluster period. A diary can help discuss patterns, but broad restrictive diets are not a proven general solution.

sections.heading: Plan support for the disruption to daily life
paragraphs: Repeated attacks can interrupt sleep, work, relationships and emotional wellbeing. Ask for an accessible written plan, follow-up during a new bout and help if pain remains uncontrolled. Discuss work adjustments and support from trusted people or a patient organisation. Severe recurrent pain deserves active care rather than dismissal as 'just a headache'. If a prescribed strategy is ineffective or difficult to use, contact the team for reassessment. Established cluster headache does not protect against an unrelated emergency, so keep the warning-sign plan alongside routine treatment.

examples.title: Repeated night attacks — hypothetical example
examples.text: A person repeatedly wakes with severe pain around the same eye and a runny nose. They bring an attack diary to assessment instead of repeatedly buying ordinary pain tablets. The clinician checks the pattern and whether other causes need investigation.

examples.title: A new eye sign — hypothetical example
examples.text: Someone with known cluster headache notices a drooping eyelid for the first time. They seek emergency assessment rather than assuming every eye symptom is explained by their old diagnosis.
